cases.title: Anglo Platinum's Mogalakwena Mine: Relocations and the Blinkwater Tailings Dam
cases.place: Sekuruwe village and Blinkwater farm, near Mokopane, Mogalakwena municipality, Limpopo, South Africa
cases.point: Blinkwater tailings dam area near Sekuruwe (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Anglo American plc (United Kingdom), through Anglo Platinum (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Owner of Anglo Platinum, whose wholly owned subsidiary Potgietersrust Platinums Ltd (PPL) runs the Mogalakwena open-pit mine and built the tailings dam on Blinkwater (Centre for Environmental Rights; London Mining Network).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The land minister signed a lease of part of Blinkwater farm to PPL on 19 January 2009 for a tailings dam; construction began that month and tailings were first pumped in on 15 July 2010 (Centre for Environmental Rights). The dam was part of a R4.5 billion expansion (London Mining Network).

companies.name: Anglo American Platinum / Potgietersrust Platinums Ltd (PPL)

cases.community: The relocation of about 10,000 residents of the neighbouring villages of Ga-Puka and Ga-Sekhaolelo was criticised by the South African Human Rights Commission, and Anglo Platinum had to apologise for removing graves without regard to custom (Miningmx). Over 100 residents of Ga-Puka and Ga-Sekhaolelo sued in 2007, saying relocation agreements were signed under duress; the court dismissed the case (EJAtlas). At Sekuruwe, the tailings dam took more than half of the community's land, including all its arable land on Blinkwater; the company fenced it off, exhumed graves and paid some farmers compensation on a take-it-or-leave-it basis (London Mining Network). The dam's footprint is about 280 ha, and 1.8 million tons of tailings had been pumped in by November 2010 (London Mining Network).
cases.ecosystem: The dam was built on the banks of the Blinkwater wetland; the community argued it had no environmental authorisation (Miningmx). Residents reported contamination of land and water (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: When 400 to 500 residents occupied the land with their cattle on 28 January 2009, police came but arrested no one; EJAtlas reports that protesters were arrested later, and Jubilee Mokopane said the company called police to arrest anyone who tried to reach their fields (EJAtlas).
cases.outcome: The Human Rights Commission investigated Anglo Platinum's mining in the area in 2008, its first inquiry into a company (EJAtlas). In 2016 Anglo American Platinum agreed to pay the Sekuruwe community compensation and build a clinic and improve water supply, after a seven-year dispute (City Press, via EJAtlas).

The arrests are reported by EJAtlas from community groups and were not found in a second source. Anglo Platinum said in 2009 that the lease was lawfully granted (EJAtlas).

cases.title: Coca-Cola's Mehdiganj Bottling Plant and the Falling Water Table
cases.place: Mehdiganj, near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
cases.point: Rajatalab, on the Grand Trunk Road in Arajiline block, Varanasi district (approximate; Mehdiganj is a village in this block just off the road, a few km from Varanasi, per India Water Portal)

lenders.name: The Coca-Cola Company (United States), through Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages, the bottling arm of Atlanta-based Coca-Cola, has run the Mehdiganj plant since 1999 (Business Standard; The Guardian/AFP).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plant. It is one of 58 Coca-Cola bottling plants in India and draws groundwater for production (The Guardian/AFP).
cases.community: Groundwater levels in Mehdiganj dropped 7.9 metres in the 11 years after bottling began, according to media reports cited by Business Standard. A 2012 study by the Central Ground Water Board found levels at the factory were the lowest in the area and labelled its water use as excess (India Resource Center). Villagers reported wells running dry, hand pumps failing and ponds drying up (India Resource Center). In June 2014 the Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board ordered the plant shut, saying it breached its licence and that its effluent contained pollutants beyond permitted limits (The Guardian/AFP).
cases.ecosystem: The pollution board said the plant's effluent held pollutants above permitted limits and ordered it to recharge twice the groundwater it had extracted (The Guardian/AFP).
cases.outcome: Earlier in 2014 local authorities said the plant was built on village council land and fined the company 126,000 rupees (about US$2,000) (The Guardian/AFP). The National Green Tribunal stayed the closure on condition that output stay at or below 600 bottles a minute until the Central Ground Water Authority cleared any increase; the company said the ruling confirmed it followed the law (Business Standard).

cases.title: Dara Sakor: Union Development Group's Coastal Concession and Evictions in Koh Kong
cases.place: Botum Sakor and Kiri Sakor districts, Koh Kong province, Cambodia
cases.point: Dara Sakor concession area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Union Development Group (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Granted a 99-year lease on 36,000 hectares on 9 May 2008 for the US$3.8 billion Dara Sakor project; the US Treasury describes it as a Chinese state-owned entity (US Treasury, 2020). RFA names its parent as Tianjin Wanlong Group.

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project. The Cambodian government leased 36,000 hectares, including part of Botum Sakor National Park, though Cambodian law limits land concessions to 10,000 hectares (US Treasury). The company registered as Cambodian-owned to receive the land, then reverted to Chinese ownership (US Treasury).
cases.community: More than 1,400 families in 12 coastal communities were moved to new villages about 20 km inland; by September 2014, 1,412 families (5,791 people) had been relocated (Drbohlav and Hejkrlik, IJAPS 2018). Relocated people reported losing access to fishing and farming areas, poor housing and land unsuitable for farming (IJAPS 2018). The US Treasury found UDG used Cambodian military forces to clear land, stopped villagers planting rice, and was accused of burning down houses (US Treasury). A UDG security guard was given a one-year suspended sentence in 2015 for punching a local woman in the face in 2014 (Cambodia Daily via Open Development Cambodia).
cases.ecosystem: Botum Sakor National Park as a whole, which holds at least nine company concessions, lost 24,500 hectares of humid primary rainforest between 2002 and 2020; satellite images show recent clearing near a road in the UDG concession (Mongabay, citing University of Maryland data).
cases.suppression: UDG used Cambodian military forces, provided through General Kun Kim, to intimidate villagers (US Treasury). In June 2023 police arrested 11 villagers on their way to petition the justice minister and charged them with incitement; previous charges were pending against 30 Koh Kong land activists (RFA, citing Licadho).
cases.outcome: The UN human rights office and Cambodia's Council of Ministers asked UDG to stop using soldiers to take land; UDG ignored a directive to stop destroying property (US Treasury). On 15 September 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned UDG under the Global Magnitsky Act for seizing and demolishing Cambodians' land (US Treasury). UDG denied plans to host Chinese military assets (Mongabay, citing VOA).

cases.title: Grande Côte Zircon Mine: Diogo Farmers Lose Land
cases.place: Diogo, Darou Khoudoss commune, Thiès region (Niayes), Senegal
cases.point: Diogo, Grande Côte Opérations mine area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Eramet (France) and Mineral Deposits Limited (Australia), through Tizir (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Tizir, a 50-50 joint venture of Eramet and Mineral Deposits Limited formed in 2011, holds 90% of Grande Côte Opérations; the Senegalese state holds 10% (Financial Afrik).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. GCO holds a 25-year renewable mining concession granted by presidential decree in November 2007 along 106 km of coast, covering Diogo, Fass Boye, Mboro and Lompoul (Financial Afrik).
cases.community: To build the plant, 465 people were compensated and another 115 were expropriated for the access road, which caused strong tension in Diogo (Financial Afrik, 2013). The sub-prefect of Méouane put the number of affected and compensated producers at 644, for 802,136,734 CFA francs; seven hamlets of Diogo and Foth were moved in February 2017 (EJAtlas). A vegetable grower told Reporterre in 2020 he now had to dig wells more than 18 metres deep, and the head of a 12-village farmers' association said GCO had promised to restore mined land (Reporterre).
cases.ecosystem: An environmental consultant told Reporterre the operation draws water from the aquifer, and a grower said wells now have to go deeper than 18 metres (Reporterre). Farmers say restored mining sites are in poor condition and planted trees struggle to grow (Reporterre).
cases.outcome: Construction was blocked for about four months in 2013 by the land dispute (Financial Afrik). GCO began production in 2014 and paid compensation above the legal scale set in 1994 (EJAtlas). In 2020 a local official said GCO had trained more than 400 young people but hired about 40 (Reporterre).

lvwhy.project: A French-Australian joint venture runs a mineral sands mine on farmland in the Niayes (Financial Afrik).

cases.title: Engen Refinery in South Durban: Pollution, Fires and Protest Bans
cases.place: Wentworth and Merebank, South Durban, eThekwini, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
cases.point: Engen refinery, Wentworth (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Petronas (Malaysia) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Bought its first Engen shares in 1996 and became majority owner in 1998; held 74% until it completed the sale of its stake to Vivo Energy in May 2024 (Free Malaysia Today/Bernama, 2024; Mail & Guardian, 2018).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the refinery. Mobil opened the Tara Road refinery in 1954 (Mail & Guardian); Petronas became Engen's majority owner in 1998 (Free Malaysia Today/Bernama).
cases.community: A 2002 health study at Settlers Primary School, between the Engen and Sapref refineries, found 52% of children had asthma, 26% of them persistent cases (New Frame). University of KwaZulu-Natal research found leukaemia 24 times higher in the valley than elsewhere in the country (Mail & Guardian, 2020). SDCEA's 2008 lawsuit cited over 120 accidents and pollution incidents at Engen since 1998; a fire in October 2011 sent more than 100 schoolchildren to hospital (EJAtlas). A 4 December 2020 explosion hospitalised six employees and two residents, burned an 11-year-old girl and forced about 28 residents out of a damaged block of flats (New Frame).
cases.ecosystem: The refinery emits sulphur dioxide and benzene into a residential area (EJAtlas). It stopped refining after the December 2020 blast and Engen announced plans to convert it to storage (Wikipedia).
cases.suppression: In 2018 police opened fire on protesters blocking refinery access (Mail & Guardian). Engen obtained a court interdict against Wentworth protest leaders using the Gatherings Act and the National Key Points Act; residents challenged the law in court in 2020 (Mail & Guardian).
cases.killed_note: No deaths are counted. The leukaemia and asthma figures describe the whole South Durban industrial basin, which also includes the Shell/BP Sapref refinery.
cases.outcome: The refinery stayed closed after the December 2020 explosion and Engen announced in 2021 that it would convert the site to a storage facility (Wikipedia, citing Reuters). In 2018 an Engen spokesperson said the company had invested R40 million in social projects in the area over five years (Mail & Guardian). Petronas sold its 74% stake to Vivo Energy in 2024 (Free Malaysia Today/Bernama).

cases.title: Golden Veroleum Palm Oil in Sinoe: Land Signed Away During Ebola
cases.place: Butaw and surrounding districts, Sinoe County, Liberia
cases.point: Butaw district, Sinoe County, within the GVL concession area (approximate)

lenders.name: Golden Agri-Resources (Singapore), through Golden Veroleum Liberia and Verdant Fund LP (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Golden Agri-Resources is the parent company of GVL (Global Witness); EJAtlas describes GVL as a subsidiary of the New York-based Verdant Fund LP. The partnership with Liberia's government was announced in August 2010 for a 220,000 ha concession plus 40,000 ha for outgrowers (EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plantation. The Liberian government granted GVL a 65-year concession, with an option for 33 more years (EJAtlas).
cases.community: In October 2012 the NGO Green Advocates filed a complaint on behalf of Sinoe communities to the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil over polluted water, bulldozed graves and forced relocation; after a January 2013 assessment the RSPO found merit and halted development until agreed benchmarks were met (EJAtlas). During the 2014 Ebola outbreak GVL held meetings encouraging illiterate residents to sign away land rights while support groups stayed home, and almost doubled its plantation (Global Witness). Liberians reported being beaten, threatened and arrested for opposing the plantation (Global Witness).
cases.ecosystem: Communities documented rivers, swamps, streams and creeks dammed, diverted or polluted, and forest cleared for planting (Forest Peoples Programme complaint, via EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: Global Witness documented violent assaults and arbitrary arrests of people who voiced concerns, and land meetings watched over by officials and, in at least one case, armed police. After a May 2015 protest by the Butaw Youth Association turned violent, with a minister wounded and a manager briefly held, police charged 23 people with offences including attempted murder (The Peninsula/AFP).
cases.outcome: GVL and GAR denied wrongdoing; GVL said it played no part in intimidation and that its 2014 operations were part of long-term plans, and GAR acknowledged "challenges" (Global Witness).

sources.title: Golden Agri Resources/Golden Veroleum Palm Oil Plantations, Sinoe, Liberia
The New Snake Oil? Violence, threats, and false promises at the heart of Liberia's palm oil expansion
Liberia charges 23 over violent plantation protest: police
'We want our land back': Liberian communities speak out about big palm oil

cases.confidence_note: The Butaw protesters themselves used violence according to police and the company. GVL denies intimidating communities (Global Witness). Global Witness reports that Standard Chartered, HSBC and Citibank held shares in GAR worth nearly US$1.5 billion (HSBC and Citibank said they held them in custody for other owners); no bank loan or bond to GAR or GVL is documented in these sources, so banks are not listed as lenders.

lvwhy.land: Customary land was signed over to a Singapore-owned plantation, much of it during the Ebola outbreak (Global Witness).

cases.title: Equatorial Palm Oil and the Jogbahn Clan in Grand Bassa
cases.place: Jogbahn clan area, District 4, Grand Bassa County, Liberia
cases.point: Equatorial Palm Oil concession area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Equatorial Palm Oil plc (United Kingdom) and Biopalm Energy (Singapore, SIVA Group) (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Equatorial Palm Oil, publicly listed in the UK, holds 50-year concessions in Grand Bassa (Mongabay); in 2011 its Liberian plantations were placed in a 50-50 joint venture with Biopalm Energy, controlled by C. Sivasankaran's SIVA Group (EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plantation. Liberia's parliament granted the concessions in 2008, totalling 169,000 ha between Buchanan and Greenville (EJAtlas).
cases.community: The company cleared forest on land the community had lived on for generations without consulting them, according to residents interviewed by Mongabay. EJAtlas reports smallholders pushed off their land, farms bulldozed and graves desecrated from 2011, and complaints of polluted drinking water.
cases.ecosystem: Forest was cleared for oil palm on the community's land (Mongabay).
cases.suppression: In September 2013 police escorted company surveyors into the villages at night. When residents dressed in white marched to petition the county supervisor, riot police beat some with sticks and used tear gas; about a dozen were driven to Buchanan and later released without charge, and four were hospitalised, according to community members (Mongabay). Global Witness found that company security and the Police Support Unit assaulted and arrested unarmed civilians; the company admitted giving logistical support to the police (Mongabay).
cases.outcome: On 5 March 2014 President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf told Jogbahn elders there would be no further EPO expansion on their land (FrontPageAfrica via farmlandgrab). EPO denied the allegations and told Mongabay it always holds dialogue with communities before working on undeveloped land.

sources.title: Equatorial Palm Oil project stalls in Bassa, Liberia
'We want our land back': Liberian communities speak out about big palm oil
Grand Bassa County celebrate halting of EPO expansion drive

cases.confidence_note: The police confirmed sending the riot unit, saying marchers threatened company property and staff; the injuries come from community members' accounts (Mongabay). EPO denied the human rights allegations.

lvwhy.land: A UK-listed plantation's expansion onto customary land was backed by riot police (Mongabay).

cases.title: Utkal Alumina in Kashipur: Alcan, Norsk Hydro and the Maikanch Shooting
cases.place: Maikanch and Kucheipadar villages, Kashipur block, Rayagada district, Odisha, India
cases.point: Maikanch village, Kashipur block, Rayagada district, where police opened fire (OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: Norsk Hydro (Norway) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: One of the original promoters of Utkal Alumina International, holding 45% until it sold its stake in 2003 (Economic Times, July 2003, quoted in the Goodland report). It was still a shareholder at the time of the December 2000 shooting; it announced its withdrawal on 17 December 2000 (EJAtlas), and the Goodland chronology says it began withdrawing in December 1999 and fully exited in 2003.

lenders.name: Alcan (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Held 35% of Utkal Alumina, rising to 45% in 2003 when it bought part of Norsk Hydro's stake; Hindalco's Indal then held 55% of the US$1 billion venture (Economic Times, July 2003, quoted in the Goodland report). Alcan was still weighing its stake in March 2007 (Goodland report).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the project. Utkal Alumina was set up in the early 1990s (the Goodland chronology says 1992) to mine bauxite in the Baphlimali hills and build an alumina refinery in Rayagada; India's March 1993 mineral policy opened mining to private investment (EJAtlas; Goodland report).
cases.community: Most affected Adivasi villagers rejected compensation, having seen earlier displacement at the nearby Nalco mine turn small farmers into slum-dwellers; police forcing them to accept compensation used baton charges, tear gas, imprisonment and torture (Goodland report, 2007). At least 25 affected villages opposed the project (Goodland report). Kashipur block is 61% Scheduled Tribe (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: The project included an open-cast bauxite mine on the Baphlimali hills and a refinery in Rayagada; the National Green Tribunal later heard a petition over mining in forest land without clearance (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: On 16 December 2000 police shot dead three Adivasis near Maikanch village (Goodland report, 2007); EJAtlas reports six people permanently disabled and 30 seriously injured. The day before, villagers had turned back a delegation of pro-project politicians at a barricade (EJAtlas). In December 2004 police baton-charged and tear-gassed more than 300 Adivasis and Dalits protesting a new police post at D-Karol, injuring at least 16 (EJAtlas). A 2006 people's tribunal found large-scale arrests, forced dispersal of meetings and midnight police raids (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: Three Adivasis shot dead by Odisha police at Maikanch on 16 December 2000 (Goodland report, 2007; EJAtlas). They are counted because the police were acting against a blockade of the project.
cases.outcome: Justice Tewatia's independent inquiry (2001) and the Justice P.K. Misra commission (2003) examined the killings (Goodland report). Tata and Norsk Hydro left the venture (Goodland report). The refinery began trial production in June 2013 (EJAtlas).

sources.publisher: Robert Goodland (via Business & Human Rights Resource Centre)

cases.confidence_note: The Goodland report was written to inform Alcan's decision on its stake. Its body text gives the shooting date once as December 2001, but its summary and chronology give 16 December 2000, as does EJAtlas. The injury figures come from EJAtlas.

lvwhy.project: A Canadian-Norwegian-Indian consortium planned a bauxite mine and refinery on Adivasi land (Goodland report).
lvwhy.land: Police pressed villagers to accept compensation and give up land for the project (Goodland report).

cases.title: Heinda Tin Mine: Thai-Owned Operator and the Myaung Pyo Floods
cases.place: Myaung Pyo village, near Myitta, Dawei district, Tanintharyi region, Myanmar
cases.point: Heinda tin mine area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Myanmar Pongpipat Co. (Thailand) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Thai firm that signed a production-sharing deal in 1999 with state-owned Mining Enterprise 2 to extract tin and tungsten from a 2,000-acre area, holding rights to 65% of output, exported to Thailand and Singapore (The Irrawaddy).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The 1999 deal gave the Thai firm a 10-year operating term; it still ran the mine in 2018 (The Irrawaddy). Permits were renewed in 2009 and 2014 without consulting villagers (EJAtlas).
cases.community: Villagers blamed years of flooding, crop damage and property loss on waste and soil dumped into Myaung Pyo Creek; Myaung Pyo has more than 500 residents, mostly farmers (The Irrawaddy). The worst flooding, from August to November 2012, destroyed 27 houses and ruined crops, and the creek, the main drinking water source, was lost to pollution (EJAtlas, citing the Dawei Pro Bono Lawyers Network). Water tests in 2013-2014 found lead 35 to 190 times and arsenic 8 times WHO drinking-water limits (EJAtlas, citing DPLN). Several villagers left for work in Thailand (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: Mine sediment washed into the watershed after heavy rains in 2008 and 2012, and pollution of Myaung Pyo creek increased with tin output (EJAtlas).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. On 19 November 2016 an unknown assailant stabbed Naw Chit Pandaing, a 22-year-old Karen activist who spoke out against mining in Dawei; the police investigation was inconclusive (EJAtlas).
cases.outcome: Nine farmers sued the two companies in 2012 for 300 million kyats (about US$227,000) (The Irrawaddy). After rulings went both ways, a nine-member Supreme Court board rejected the suit in February 2018 under the Limitation Act (The Irrawaddy; EJAtlas). The Karen National Union, which controls the area, ordered the company to halt mining, but it did not comply (The Irrawaddy).

sources.title: Heinda tin mine, Dawei, Myanmar
Farmers Lose Lengthy Court Battle Against Thai, Govt Mine

cases.confidence_note: The water test results and the 27 destroyed houses come from a lawyers' network report cited by EJAtlas. The courts found the claim time-barred and did not rule on the damage itself; the High Court agreed there was a valid cause of action in negligence (EJAtlas). The Irrawaddy dates the first filing to 2012; EJAtlas gives 9 May 2014.

lvwhy.project: A Thai firm took 65% of a state tin mine whose waste flooded the village downstream (The Irrawaddy).

cases.title: Golden Lead Fishmeal Factory in Gunjur: Red Lagoon and Arrests
cases.place: Gunjur and the Bolong Fenyo reserve, West Coast Region, The Gambia
cases.point: Golden Lead factory, Gunjur (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Golden Lead (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Chinese-owned company granted a 99-year lease in 2015 to run the first Chinese fishmeal factory in The Gambia, at Gunjur (BBC).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the factory. The lease was granted under President Yahya Jammeh, soon after The Gambia broke ties with Taiwan (BBC).

companies.name: Golden Lead Import and Export Trade Company

cases.community: On 22 May 2017, about a year after the factory opened, the lagoon in the Bolong Fenyo wildlife reserve filled with dead fish and turned deep red (BBC). Fishermen say stocks have fallen and the factory buys in bulk at US$5 a basket, a third of the local market price, leaving less fish for local people (BBC). Fishermen and workers reported skin problems after entering the sea near the factory, though the BBC found no definitive evidence linking them to it. Promised jobs, a road and a fish market were not delivered, according to Gunjur's village chief (BBC).
cases.ecosystem: The National Environment Agency alleged factory wastewater caused the 2017 die-off in the Bolong Fenyo lagoon, a protected wetland (BBC).
cases.suppression: In March 2018 villagers removed a factory pipe they said was pumping waste into the ocean; five of those involved, including activist Lamin Jassey, were later arrested and put on trial (The Ecologist).
cases.outcome: In June 2017 the National Environment Agency took Golden Lead to court; the company paid US$25,000 in an out-of-court settlement and was ordered to treat its wastewater (BBC; The Ecologist). In 2023 a former senior fisheries official was jailed for two years for taking payments from Golden Lead between 2018 and 2020 (BBC). Golden Lead said the pipe removed by villagers was no longer in use (The Ecologist).

cases.confidence_note: The link between the factory and the 2017 die-off rests on the environment agency's allegation, settled out of court. Overfishing is also driven by foreign trawlers and other factories (BBC).

lvwhy.project: A Chinese-owned factory turns local fish into export fishmeal beside a protected lagoon (BBC).

cases.title: Kun Hou Mining on the Ulindi River: Guns and Cash for Armed Groups
cases.place: Ulindi River, Shabunda territory, South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo
cases.point: Ulindi River near Shabunda (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Kun Hou Mining (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Chinese-owned company running mechanised gold dredges on the Ulindi River (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik and The EastAfrican).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the dredging. South Kivu's provincial government kept supporting Kun Hou despite repeated legal violations and requests from the national government to shut it down (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik). EJAtlas says neither the company nor the artisanal miners held mining licences.

companies.name: Alfa Gold Corp DMCC
companies.role: Buyer of gold via a Bukavu trading house

cases.community: Raia Mutomboki armed groups received at least two AK-47 rifles and US$4,000 in cash from Kun Hou, and made up to US$25,000 a month extorting artisanal miners (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik). Up to US$17 million of gold produced by Kun Hou in one year was likely smuggled out of the country, and Global Witness said over 500 malnutrition cases were reported in Shabunda town in 2014 (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik). EJAtlas reports the armed groups threatened, robbed and beat local people and miners.
cases.ecosystem: Each dredge uses at least two kilograms of mercury a week, according to the regional civil society coalition COSOC-GL (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: Armed groups paid by the company controlled the river and taxed miners, in a tax-sharing deal with local authorities (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik).
cases.outcome: In March and June 2015 Prime Minister Matata Ponyo told the South Kivu governor to stop all dredging on the river (EJAtlas). Congo's mines minister called for a clean-up of the gold sector after the Global Witness report (EJAtlas). A French employee named in the documents could not be reached, and Alfa Gold did not respond (Global Witness, via Financial Afrik).

cases.title: Loliondo: A UAE Hunting Concession and Repeated Maasai Evictions

lenders.name: Otterlo Business Corporation (United Arab Emirates) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Granted exclusive hunting rights in 1992 over an area of 400,000 hectares, in a deal reported to involve millions of dollars to Tanzania's armed forces (Conservation Watch); Amnesty International says the government leased the whole of Loliondo division as a hunting block to a UAE company in 1992. In 2022 the Guardian reported that the land being demarcated was for a reserve to be operated by a UAE-owned company.

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the concession. Tanzania granted the hunting block to OBC in 1992; a minister said in 2017 that OBC would never receive another hunting licence, but a 2022 update said OBC had not left (Conservation Watch).

companies.name: Otterlo Business Corporation (OBC)
companies.role: Holder of the Loliondo hunting concession

cases.community: In 2009 more than 200 Maasai homes were burned, leaving villagers without food, land, water or shelter, according to UN Special Rapporteur James Anaya (Conservation Watch). In June 2022 more than 70,000 Maasai were at risk of losing their grazing land as 1,500 square kilometres were demarcated (Amnesty International).

Ten Maasai leaders were detained, and people injured crossed into Kenya for treatment to avoid arrest (The Guardian).
cases.killed_note: No death is counted. One police officer was killed in the June 2022 clashes; the government said villagers killed him (Al Jazeera).
cases.outcome: In 2018 the East African Court of Justice ordered the state not to evict the Maasai until their case was decided (Amnesty International). The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights condemned the 2022 violence (Al Jazeera). The government denied evicting anyone, said the area was being set aside for conservation, and said the Maasai keep access to 2,500 square kilometres (The Guardian; Al Jazeera).

cases.title: Aswan High Dam: Soviet Credits and the Displacement of the Nubians
cases.place: Lower Nubia, Aswan governorate, Egypt, and Wadi Halfa, Sudan
cases.point: Aswan High Dam (Wikipedia coordinates)

lenders.name: Soviet Union (government credits)
lenders.role: Agreed in October 1958 to lend 400 million rubles to finance the first phase of the High Dam, with repayment reported to run 12 years (US State Department cables, Foreign Relations of the United States 1958-1960); in January 1960 Egypt announced the USSR would finance the second stage on the same basis (FRUS). Wikipedia, citing a 1971 CIA report, puts the Soviet credits at about US$425 million covering the project's foreign-exchange costs.

cases.conditions: The United States, the United Kingdom and the World Bank (IBRD) withdrew their support in 1956 (Wikipedia). The Soviet credits paid for the first and then the second stage of the dam (FRUS). The dam was designed by the Moscow-based Hydroproject Institute (Wikipedia).
cases.community: Lake Nasser flooded much of Lower Nubia, and 100,000 to 120,000 people were resettled in Egypt and Sudan (Wikipedia). In Sudan, 50,000 to 70,000 Nubians were moved from Wadi Halfa, some 700 km south to the Butana plain; in Egypt most of the 50,000 Nubians were moved near Kom Ombo (Wikipedia). Residents of 44 Nubian villages were forced into temporary shelters in 1963-1964 (EJAtlas). Amnesty International says those moved from the Nile banks to desert areas often could no longer farm.
cases.ecosystem: Silt now settles in Lake Nasser; Egypt's Mediterranean catch fell from 35,000-40,000 tons a year to 20,000 tons or less as the sardine population disappeared, and coastal erosion increased (Wikipedia, citing a 1971 CIA report; figures not checked against the report itself).
cases.suppression: On 3 September 2017 police beat Nubian marchers in Aswan who were calling for the return to their land, and arrested 24 men (Amnesty International).
cases.outcome: A provision in the 2014 constitution recognises the Nubians' right to return (Amnesty International). In 2016 the government offered 922 acres of former Nubian land at Khorqandi and Toshka to investors (EJAtlas). Egypt began compensating Nubians who lost homes in 2019-2020 (Wikipedia).

cases.title: Alamos Gold's Kirazlı Mine: Forest Felled on Mount Ida
cases.place: Kirazlı, near Mount Ida (Kaz Dağları), Çanakkale province, Turkey
cases.point: Kirazlı project area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Alamos Gold (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Toronto-based miner that acquired the Kirazlı and Ağı Dağı projects in 2010 and was active in Turkey through Dutch subsidiaries (Mining.com; EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The energy ministry gave permission to start construction in 2019 (EJAtlas); the Kirazlı open-pit mine was planned to use cyanide (Hürriyet Daily News).
cases.community: Opponents held a large protest march at Kirazlı on 5 August 2019, and a TEMA Foundation petition had about 500,000 signatures by 8 August (EJAtlas). Opposition grew over allegations that the company had cut more trees than its environmental impact report allowed and over its plan to use cyanide in a densely forested area (Mining.com; Hürriyet Daily News). The project lies in the same water basin as the Atikhisar Dam, the only water source for 180,000 people (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: The TEMA Foundation, a Turkish environmental NGO, calculated that the company cut almost 195,000 trees, four times the number declared in the impact assessment; this is TEMA's estimate, reported by EJAtlas, and the company is said to have cut them "allegedly". In 2021 forestry ministry officials, asked about the 350,000 trees cut in the area, said the damaged site could be rehabilitated (Hürriyet Daily News).
cases.outcome: The Çanakkale administrative court suspended exploration in December 2013 (EJAtlas). Work stopped in 2019 after protests and the expiry of the mining permit (Mining.com). In March 2021 the forestry ministry revoked the licence on the grounds that it had not been extended (Hürriyet Daily News); Alamos said the government had failed to grant a routine renewal for 18 months, sought more than US$1 billion from Turkey under the Netherlands-Turkey investment treaty, and denied that cyanide would leak (Mining.com).

cases.title: Bangka Island: A Hong Kong-Owned Iron Ore Mine Against the Courts
cases.place: Bangka Island, North Minahasa regency, North Sulawesi, Indonesia
cases.point: Bangka Island (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Aempire Resource Ltd (Hong Kong), through PT Mikgro Metal Perdana (foreign investor)
lenders.role: PT MMP, a local subsidiary of Hong Kong-based Aempire Resource, held an exploration permit from 2008 covering nearly half the island (Mongabay, 2016).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The district head granted the permit; Indonesia's 2007 small-islands law forbids mining on islands under 200,000 hectares, and Bangka is under 5,000 hectares (Asia Pacific Report).
cases.community: Bangka has about 3,000 residents who live from fishing, crops and marine tourism (EJAtlas). Villagers said mining would force them to relocate and destroy the forest and sea they depend on (Mongabay, 2014). JATAM reported that land was cleared, mangroves buried and coral reefs destroyed to build roads, a port and warehouses (Asia Pacific Report, via UCA News).
cases.ecosystem: A local NGO reported deforestation and infilling of mangroves in the company's work area (Mongabay, 2016). The island lies in the Coral Triangle near Bunaken Marine Park (Mongabay, 2014).
cases.suppression: On 18 February 2014, when hundreds of villagers and fishermen tried to stop an MMP ship unloading heavy machinery, armed police reportedly levelled their weapons at protesters; one protest boat was destroyed when a water taxi collided with it, and its four occupants were rescued with minor injuries (Mongabay, 2014).
cases.outcome: The High Administrative Court in Makassar revoked the permits in March 2013 and the Supreme Court dismissed the company's appeal in September 2013; the district still let the company work, and the energy minister granted an operations permit in 2014, which residents also defeated in court (Mongabay, 2016). In 2017 the energy minister revoked MMP's licence (Asia Pacific Report).

cases.title: Rui Feng Sugar Concessions on Kuoy Land in Preah Vihear
cases.place: Tbeng Meanchey and Chheb districts, Preah Vihear province, Cambodia
cases.point: Preah Vihear provincial town, Tbeng Meanchey district, near the Kuoy villages of Pra Me commune (approximate)

lenders.name: Hengfu Group Sugar Industry (China), through Rui Feng (Cambodia) International and four sister companies (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Five subsidiaries of Guangdong-based Hengfu Group received more than 40,000 hectares in five 70-year land concessions in 2011, which allowed the group to get around the 10,000-hectare legal limit per company (RFA). Rui Feng opened a US$360 million sugar mill there in 2016 (Phnom Penh Post via farmlandgrab; RFA).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plantations. The Cambodian government granted the concessions in 2011; Rui Feng's 9,000 hectares were later reduced by 1,000 hectares amid land disputes (RFA).

companies.name: Hengfu Group Sugar Industry Co., Ltd.

cases.community: From 2012 Rui Feng began bulldozing land and forest the Kuoy minority used for farming, and a Kuoy representative said living standards had "dramatically declined" (RFA). Villagers said they were forced into mill jobs as resources disappeared, some children left school to guard farmland, and authorities never paid fair compensation (RFA). Punlok Khmer, a civil society group, estimated that some 1,000 families in 20 villages had been directly affected since 2012, and Chheb residents said forest and creek income (mushrooms, resin, fruit, fish) had largely dried up (RFA). The companies cleared community forest and valuable resin trees without an impact assessment (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: Community forests, including resin trees, were cleared for sugarcane (EJAtlas).
cases.suppression: Villagers, NGO staff and monks were held by police on several occasions, and the company sued villagers for destroying sugarcane (EJAtlas, citing the Phnom Penh Post). In 2016 police stopped more than 200 Kuoy villagers who wanted to give Prime Minister Hun Sen a petition at the mill's opening (Phnom Penh Post via farmlandgrab).
cases.outcome: The provincial governor said disputes were resolved by trimming the concession and returning land to residents; villagers disputed this (RFA). Hun Sen told Rui Feng not to expand onto new land (Phnom Penh Post via farmlandgrab). Kuoy villagers filed a lawsuit seeking US$600,000 in compensation (EJAtlas).

cases.title: Nordgold's Bissa Gold Mine: Two Villages Moved

lenders.name: Nordgold (Russia) (foreign investor)

In April 2016 a group of women blocked national road N22 for at least a day, accusing Bissa Gold of taking their land without employing their children (Burkina state news agency AIB, via aOuaga).
cases.outcome: Nordgold said the relocations followed best practice, that it built seven new wells for 2,050 people, tests well water every three months, and that the NGO report relied on inaccurate anecdotal evidence (Nordgold response, 2016).

cases.place: Kalsaka department, Yatenga province, and Séguénéga, Burkina Faso
cases.point: Kalsaka mine area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Cluff Gold plc / Amara Mining plc (United Kingdom) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Cluff Mining arrived in Kalsaka in 2006 and was later replaced by Amara Mining (WoMin and ORCADE); Amara's subsidiaries KMSA and SMSA mined Kalsaka/Sega from 2008 to August 2014 (Amara Mining response).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. The Burkina Faso state held 10% (EJAtlas). After mining stopped, SMSA went into liquidation in December 2014 and KMSA into court-supervised creditor protection (Amara Mining response).

companies.name: Amara Mining plc (formerly Cluff Gold plc)
Kalsaka Mining SA (KMSA) and Sega Mining SA (SMSA)

cases.community: Industrial mining ended both farming and artisanal mining for many of the 51 villages around Kalsaka; a security company barred artisanal miners from the gold site, and expropriated farmers called their cash compensation inadequate (WoMin and ORCADE). Compensation covered only fields, not lost panning sites, and women were hit hardest (WoMin and ORCADE). The 2013 move to the Sega deposit involved displacements, and a new road cut villages off from their fields (EJAtlas).
cases.ecosystem: In August 2016, two years after mining stopped, a visiting minister found open pits 80 to 120 metres deep at the Kalsaka and Séguénéga sites, and the company's deputy managing director said regulations were holding up restoration work, to be paid from a rehabilitation fund of more than 1.65 billion CFA francs (Sidwaya). EJAtlas also reports the pits had not been rehabilitated, leaving degraded farmland.
cases.outcome: Amara said its subsidiaries paid compensation to farmers affected by the Sega deposit under a relocation action plan, supported programmes for women, and were focused on closing the mine with all environmental obligations fulfilled (Amara Mining response, 2016). Perseus, Amara's later owner, remains responsible for restoring the sites (EJAtlas).

cases.title: Syrah's Balama Graphite Mine: Unpaid Land Compensation and a Police Raid
cases.place: Mualia community, Balama district, Cabo Delgado, Mozambique
cases.point: Balama graphite mine (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Syrah Resources (Australia), through Twigg Exploration and Mining (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Melbourne-listed Syrah owns 95% of the Balama graphite complex, run by its subsidiary Twigg (EJAtlas; Evidências).

cases.title: Alpha Cement Factory: Rubber Bullets and Arrests at Aung Thabyay

lenders.role: Joint-venture partner with Myanmar's Myint Investment Group in the Alpha Cement plant, which was being upgraded to 5,000 tonnes a day (Global Cement, May 2019); RFA in 2024 described the plant as owned by Myint Investment Group and Anhui Conch Cement. cases.title: Green Resources Plantations in Uganda: Evictions at Bukaleba and Kachung
cases.place: Bukaleba Central Forest Reserve (Mayuge district) and Kachung Central Forest Reserve (Dokolo district), Uganda
cases.point: Bukaleba Central Forest Reserve (EJAtlas map point); Kachung lies about 170 km north

lenders.name: International Finance Corporation (IFC)
lenders.role: IFC project 26506 proposed a US$10 million A loan and a US$6.5 million C loan, plus a carbon delivery guarantee, for Green Resources' three-year programme to expand plantations in Tanzania, Uganda and Mozambique and modernise a Tanzanian sawmill; approved 20 April 2009, signed 1 May 2009, invested 15 March 2010 (IFC disclosure).

lenders.name: Norfund (Norway) and Finnfund (Finland)
lenders.role: State development finance institutions; Norfund had provided US$7 million in loans to Green Resources and a further US$25 million together with Finnfund, according to a 2014 report (Oakland Institute). The dates of these loans are not given in that report.

cases.conditions: The IFC-backed programme included planting 9,000 hectares of eucalyptus, pine, teak and indigenous trees and obtaining FSC and CDM certification (IFC project 26506). Green Resources holds 50-year licences on 9,165 ha at Bukaleba (1996) and 2,670 ha at Kachung (1999) (EJAtlas).
cases.community: Upwards of 8,000 people faced profound disruption to their livelihoods under the licence agreements, including forced evictions (estimates of those affected range from 8,000 to 40,000); one village described an eviction driven by "people with guns" (Oakland Institute, 2014). The company added 530 hectares at Kachung and 889 at Bukaleba in 2011-2012, worsening land shortages for food (Oakland Institute). cases.suppression: Community members named government employees, the army, military and police as responsible for forced evictions, and reported being harassed, fined and jailed for trespass on licensed land (Oakland Institute).
cases.outcome: On 3 November 2015 the Swedish Energy Agency froze further payments for Kachung carbon credits after a Swedish TV4 programme on land conflicts (EJAtlas).

cases.title: Korindo's Oil Palm in Papua: Forest Cleared and Land Rights Violated
cases.place: Boven Digoel and Merauke regencies, Papua, Indonesia
cases.point: Korindo plantation area, southern Papua (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Korindo Group (South Korea) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Korean-founded conglomerate and the largest oil palm company in Papua, with about 149,000 ha of plantations through eight subsidiaries (EJAtlas); Mongabay describes it as an Indonesian-South Korean joint venture.

cases.conditions: No lender's terms are documented. Korindo held forest release permits for its subsidiaries, such as 34,100 ha for PT Donghin Prabhawa (EJAtlas).
cases.community: An FSC investigation found "clear and convincing evidence" that Korindo violated indigenous Papuans' rights by failing to consult them properly and paying unfair compensation, received by a minority only; communities suffered harms ranging from threats and some use of violence to an atmosphere of intimidation (FSC findings, via Mongabay). cases.community: Forty-nine children in Kangqiao, most aged one to three, were diagnosed with excessive blood lead in 2011, and three were still in hospital in February 2012 (AFP via Phys.org). cases.place: Ogbodo, Isiokpo, Ikwerre local government area, Rivers State, Nigeria
cases.point: Isiokpo town, Ikwerre local government area; Ogbodo is a village of Isiokpo (approximate)

lenders.name: Royal Dutch Shell (Netherlands/United Kingdom), through Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria (foreign investor)
lenders.role: SPDC, Shell's Nigerian subsidiary, owned the pipeline that burst at Ogbodo (Cultural Survival; Weekly Trust via AllAfrica).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the pipeline. SPDC found oil in commercial quantities at Ogbodo in 1972 (EJAtlas).

companies.name: Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria (SPDC)

cases.community: A pipeline explosion in June 2001 caused an 18-day spill that covered the community's waterways and much of its farmland; residents went over a month without adequate water for drinking, bathing or cooking (Cultural Survival; Africa Action). cases.title: CDC's Oil Palm Investment at Manis Mata: Dayak Land Taken
cases.place: Manis Mata sub-district, Ketapang district, West Kalimantan, Indonesia
cases.point: Manis Mata, PT HSL concession area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: CDC (Commonwealth Development Corporation, United Kingdom)
lenders.role: The British government's development finance institution invested US$3.3 million in equity and lent US$13.5 million for the plantation, mill and bulking station, and helped prepare the feasibility study; in mid-1999 it signed a further US$32 million investment, took 65% of the business and became its manager (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar, 2000).

cases.conditions: CDC described its initial 1996 investment as a 6,000-hectare plantation; by mid-1999 it had become a total plantation of 25,400 ha, including 4,000 ha under a smallholder scheme (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). The UK Department for International Development then held all of CDC's shares (Down to Earth).
cases.community: The concessions cover customary land of 15 Dayak Jelai and Melayu communities (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). A 2000 field investigation found land taken without consent, burning and bulldozing, desecration of graves and unfair compensation; one woman lost about 30 ha without compensation, and families who handed over 14 ha received a 2-ha stake in the plantation co-operative (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). In Keladi about 120 families gave up land but only 51 received co-operative plots in the first phase; some villagers had waited five years for compensation (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar).
cases.ecosystem: Fires apparently set by PT HSL or its contractors in September 1994, before CDC invested, burned villagers' tree crops at Beriam, including 25,000 native rubber and 20,000 durian trees, before the land was bulldozed (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). Since the CDC-financed processing mill opened in 1998, villagers have reported water pollution from poor waste management and concerns over air pollution (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar).
cases.suppression: The company used the village administration's ties to police and military in the Suharto era to force communities to hand over land (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). After villagers cut down about 400 oil palms in July 2000, extra police were sent from Ketapang and a planned follow-up NGO visit was cancelled because of police measures (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar).
cases.outcome: In mid-1999 villagers reoccupied about 2,000 ha of the plantation, marking plots with their names (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). A local government team (TP3DII) reported some grounds for the villagers' complaints, including few co-operative plots allocated and compensation owed (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar). The plantation was later owned by Cargill and Temasek (EJAtlas).

sources.title: Manis Mata conflict (PT HSL) in Kalimantan, Indonesia

sources.publisher: Down to Earth and WALHI Kalimantan Barat

cases.confidence_note: The harm findings come from one two-week field investigation by WALHI Kalbar and Down to Earth (2000), which did not approach the company directly; it reports the government TP3DII team's findings. CDC's stakes are taken from CDC's own reports as quoted there. The 1994 fires and much of the land taking (1993-1996) came before or as CDC first invested in 1996; CDC's larger 1999 investment, which gave it 65% and management control, came while the disputes were unresolved, and the 2000 police reinforcement and unpaid compensation fall in its period.

lvwhy.land: Dayak customary land was converted to oil palm for a CDC-owned company (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar).
lvwhy.finance: CDC equity and loans financed the plantation and mill (Down to Earth and WALHI Kalbar).

cases.title: Nordgold's Lefa Mine: Cyanide Spill at Fayalala Carrefour
cases.place: Fayalala Carrefour village, Lèro, Siguiri prefecture, Guinea
cases.point: Lefa gold mine area (EJAtlas map point)

lenders.name: Nordgold (Russia) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Holds 85% of Société Minière de Dinguiraye, which runs the Lefa mine (BankTrack); Nordgold acquired the mine in July 2010 (EJAtlas).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine. Commercial production began in 2008 under Crew Gold, and Nordgold acquired the mine in July 2010 (EJAtlas).
cases.community: In the first half of July 2015 the tailings settling pond overflowed into the lake the village used for domestic water, and drinking water has been hard to get since (Kolie et al., 2019, citing Guinéenews; BankTrack). Fayalala Carrefour has about 1,700 people living a few hundred metres from the tailings (Kolie et al., 2019). In a 2013 survey of 961 respondents, 31% said the mine had polluted or degraded farmland and 28% reported the loss of plant and animal species (Kolie et al., 2019). Blasting damaged homes, and the village has asked for years to be relocated (BankTrack).
cases.ecosystem: Of 24 plant species recorded before the mine, many became rare or disappeared in the concession and nearby villages (Kolie et al., 2019).
cases.outcome: Attempts by the village to negotiate relocation with SMD had repeatedly failed by May 2023 (BankTrack). BankTrack noted that on 25 March 2021 Nordgold entered a two-year US$100 million ESG-linked revolving credit facility with international banks including Deutsche Bank, and asked Deutsche Bank to suspend further finance to Nordgold (BankTrack). EJAtlas reports that the company said it would relocate the village to expand the mine.
